entities.summary:
Nahariya, established in 1935, emerged as the northernmost coastal city of Israel, a pioneering agricultural settlement founded by German-Jewish immigrants fleeing Nazi persecution during the Fifth Aliyah. Conceived as a utopian agrarian community named 'Nahariya Smallholders' Settlement Association' by engineers Joseph Loewy, Dr. Selmar Hirsch, and Dr. Werner Samson, alongside financial backing from Alfred and Paul Marcus, it rapidly transformed the coastal plains of the Western Galilee. Its strategic location on the Mediterranean coast, approximately 10 kilometers north of Acre, positioned it as a crucial gateway to the northern reaches of Mandatory Palestine, embodying the Zionist vision of reclaiming and cultivating the land.

Initially focused on dairy farming, citrus groves, and vegetable cultivation, Nahariya quickly adapted its economic model as the realities of the market and the influx of new settlers demanded diversification. During World War II, its character shifted dramatically when the British Mandate authorities established significant military bases and infrastructure in and around the settlement, including an airfield and naval facilities. This transformation brought an economic boom, drawing labor and services, and laying the groundwork for its subsequent urbanization. Post-1948, following Israel's independence, Nahariya absorbed a wave of Holocaust survivors and immigrants from various countries, rapidly expanding its population and developing industrial zones, notably in textiles and food processing, alongside its enduring agricultural base.
